title: Yuki-Onna
subtitle: Lafcadio Hearn's snow woman (1904) — a promise made in a storm, and the night it is broken.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
intention: you'll tell a Japanese ghost story of a promise and its price, and use conditionals for warnings, threats and promises — and the mixed conditional for looking back at what a broken promise cost.
warmup: Think of a promise that was very hard to keep. What made it hard — and was it kept?
Every culture has a figure that lives in the cold or the dark and is not quite human. What is it where you grew up?
If someone spares your life on one condition, do you owe them that condition forever?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Do the thinking first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: At eighteen he was still an apprentice: he carried the tools, watched the old man's hands, and was paid almost nothing while he learned.
items.meaning: an apprentice (n) — a young person learning a trade by working for a skilled master.

items.sent: They had walked for an hour under a clear sky when the storm overtook them, and within minutes they could not see the road.
items.meaning: to overtake (v) — to catch up with and pass; of weather or events, to come upon someone suddenly.

items.sent: The ferryman found the boy lying senseless in the snow; it was an hour before he opened his eyes and asked where he was.
When she saw the letter she shrieked so loudly that the neighbours came running.
items.meaning: to shriek (v) — to give a high, piercing cry, from fear, anger or pain.

vocab.heading: B. From the meaning to the word
vocab.instruction: Which word fits the definition? The first letter is given. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: Which word means 'formally engaged to be married' — old-fashioned and rather solemn? It begins with b.
items.meaning: betrothed (adj) — engaged to be married. She was already betrothed to a merchant's son.

items.sent: Which verb means 'to promise formally, to bind yourself with your word'? It begins with p.
items.meaning: to pledge (v) — to promise solemnly; pledged to marry, pledged to silence.

items.sent: Which verb means 'to make a sound with your voice, to say anything at all' — usually in the negative? It begins with u.
items.meaning: to utter (v) — to make a sound or say a word. He could not utter a sound.

vocab.heading: C. Complete the chunk
vocab.instruction: These words live inside fixed phrases. Say the missing word, then reveal.

items.sent: When the rain began, the travellers took ___ under a bridge.
items.meaning: to take shelter — to go somewhere protected from weather or danger. (shelter, n/v)

items.sent: His mother took a sudden ___ to the girl and would not let her leave.
items.meaning: to take a fancy to someone — to start liking someone suddenly and strongly.

items.sent: By the end of the journey the two strangers were exchanging ___ — the kind of private things you tell only a friend.
items.meaning: confidences (n, plural) — private thoughts or secrets shared in trust. to exchange confidences

vocab_use: Put the ten words in the order you'd expect them to appear in a ghost story that ends in a marriage. Say why.
Using any three of the words, predict what happens between the two woodcutters and the woman in white.
story_intro: Hearn's own text, lightly shortened. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — The hut in the storm

paras.from: In a village of Musashi Province
skip: Several times a bridge was built

check.q: Why do the two woodcutters end up in the ferryman's hut, and what is wrong with it as a shelter?
check.a: A snowstorm overtakes them on the way home, the boatman has left the boat on the far bank, and the hut has no fire, no brazier and no window — only a door they fasten shut.

check.q: What exactly does the woman in white do to Mosaku, and what condition does she set for Minokichi?
check.a: She bends over the old man and blows her bright white breath on him — he is found frozen dead. She spares Minokichi because he is young, on condition that he never tells anyone, even his mother, what he saw; if he does, she will kill him.

story.discuss: She says she 'cannot help feeling some pity' for him because he is young and 'pretty'. Is that mercy — or is it something colder? What does the condition she sets tell us about her?

story.title: Part 2 — The girl on the road

paras.from: By dawn the storm was over
paras.to: she had first come to the village.
replace:
_Ki ga aréba, mé mo kuchi hodo
ni mono wo iu:_
Ki ga areba, me mo kuchi hodo ni mono wo iu:

check.q: Who is O-Yuki, according to what she tells Minokichi on the road — and where is she going?
check.a: A tall, good-looking girl who says she has recently lost both parents and is travelling to Yedo, where poor relations might find her work as a servant.

check.q: Give two details from this part that quietly hint O-Yuki is not an ordinary woman.
check.a: Her ten children are all 'very fair of skin'; and while peasant women age early, she looks as young and fresh after ten children as on the day she arrived — the villagers think her 'by nature different'.

story.discuss: Hearn never says the girl on the road is the woman from the hut — he lets the reader work it out. Where exactly did you become sure? Which clue did it for you?

story.title: Part 3 — By the light of the lamp

paras.from: One night, after the children had gone to sleep

check.q: What makes Minokichi break his silence after all these years?
check.a: Watching O-Yuki sewing with the lamp on her face reminds him of the beautiful white woman in the hut — she looks so like her that he starts to tell the story, still unsure whether it was a dream.

check.q: Why does O-Yuki not kill him, and what does she demand instead?
check.a: Only because of the children asleep in the room. She orders him to take very good care of them, warning that if they ever have reason to complain of him she will come back and treat him as he deserves — then she melts into white mist and is never seen again.

story.discuss: He didn't tell 'anybody' in the ordinary sense — he told her. Did Minokichi actually break his promise? Argue it both ways.

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: warnings, promises — and looking back
grammar.intro: The whole story hangs on one sentence spoken in a hut: if you ever tell anybody… I will kill you. That is a conditional used as a threat. At the end we look back at what breaking it cost — and that needs a different conditional.
notes:
1. Warnings, threats and promises — the first conditional at full strength.
• If + present simple, will / shall + verb: "If you touch that door again, I will lock it."
• ever makes the warning total: "If you ever come back here, you'll regret it."
• unless = if… not: "I'll say nothing unless you force me to."
• Formal or old-fashioned: Should + subject + verb (no if): "Should anyone ask, I was never here."

2. Looking back — what a broken promise cost.
• Third conditional (past → past): "If the coach had listened, the team would have won."
• Mixed conditional (past → present): "If the coach had listened, the team would still be in the league today."
The if-clause stays in the past perfect; the result clause tells you whether you're talking about then (would have…) or now (would… now / still / today).

exercises.h3: Warnings and promises — put the verbs in the right form
exercises.instruction: Present simple after if / unless / should; will in the result. Read each one aloud as a threat or a promise.
items: If you ___ (ever / tell) a soul, I ___ (know).
Unless the boatman ___ (come back), we ___ (have to) sleep here.
If she ___ (not / find) work in the city, her relations ___ (turn) her away.
Should the storm ___ (get) worse tonight, the hut ___ (not / hold).
exercises.note: Notice 4: after Should the verb is the bare infinitive — should the storm get — because should is doing the job of if.

exercises.h3: Looking back — third and mixed conditionals
exercises.instruction: Decide whether the result is in the past (would have…) or now (would… still / today).
items: If Minokichi ___ (keep) his word, O-Yuki ___ (still / sit) beside him today.
If the old man ___ (not / fall) asleep so fast, he ___ (might / see) the woman too.
She ___ (never / spare) him if he ___ (be) as old as Mosaku.
If O-Yuki ___ (not / love) the children, she ___ (kill) him that night.
answers: had kept / would still be sitting (would still sit)
had not fallen / might have seen
would never have spared / had been
had not loved / would have killed
exercises.note: 1 is mixed (a past 'if', a present result — today); 2, 3 and 4 are third conditionals — the result is back in the past.

exercises.instruction: One each, from: Should · unless · as long as · in case · even if. Number 1 is formal and contains no if.
items: ___ you ever mention this night, I shall hear of it.
I will not harm you ___ you break your word.
You may stay in this house ___ you are good to my children.
Bring the wood inside ___ the storm returns tonight.
___ she looks eighteen, she is not a girl at all.
exercises.note: in case = because it might happen; even if = it makes no difference whether.

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll use both halves: the threat as it was made in the hut, and the mixed conditional to say what it cost twenty years later.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Lafcadio Hearn was a Greek-Irish journalist who arrived in Japan in 1890, married into a samurai family, took the name Koizumi Yakumo and spent his last fourteen years writing down the ghost stories ordinary people told him. Kwaidan (1904) was his last collection; he heard Yuki-Onna, he said, from a farmer in Musashi. He died the year it was published.

The story is built on a trap that closes slowly. The threat is made in the first scene, and then the story goes quiet for twenty years — a marriage, ten children, a mother-in-law's dying blessing. We forget the threat. Minokichi forgets it too; that is exactly why he speaks. And when the snow woman finally reveals herself, she does not carry out her sentence. She is stopped by the same thing that stopped her in the hut: pity. The monster keeps her word better than the man keeps his.
deeper.note: Look again at the last paragraph. Her voice 'became thin, like a crying of wind' and she 'melted into a bright white mist'. Hearn never says she died, or fled, or was destroyed. What do you think happened to her?
questions: The story could be read as a horror story, a love story, or a story about marriage — about the one thing you must never say to the person you live with. Which reading is truest to the text?
O-Yuki has two conditions: the first ("never tell") and the last ("take care of the children"). Compare them. What has changed in her between the hut and the lamp?
Minokichi says he was 'never sure whether it was a dream'. Is that an excuse, or an honest confusion? Does it change his guilt?
Hearn collected this from a farmer. What do you think a story like this was for in a village — a warning, a comfort, an explanation of something?

speak.useful: The threat as she made it: "If you ever…, I will…", "Should you ever…, I shall…", "…unless…". Looking back: "If he had kept his word, she would still…", "If she hadn't loved the children, she would have…". For opinions: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "On one level… but on another…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell Yuki-Onna to someone who has never heard it. Move through the arc: the storm and the hut → the woman in white and her warning → the girl on the road → ten children and a wife who never ages → the lamp, the confession, the mist.

Quote the threat as a conditional, and finish with one mixed conditional about what it cost. Use at least five key words (apprentice, overtake, take shelter, utter, senseless, betrothed, pledge, take a fancy to, confidences, shriek).

tasks.label: Task B · Betrayal, or love? (4 minutes)
paras: Minokichi broke a promise that had kept him alive — but he broke it because he was looking at his wife and thinking she was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. Build an argument: was the confession a betrayal, an act of love, or simple carelessness? Then argue the opposite side for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · A promise with a price (4 minutes)
paras: Tell a story — real, famous, or invented — in which everything depends on one promise or one condition, and say what happened when it was tested. Use conditionals to state the condition and to look back at the result.
menu: Orpheus, who could bring his wife back from the dead as long as he did not look behind him — and looked.
Bluebeard's wife, given every key in the castle but forbidden to open one door.
A confidentiality agreement at work: the colleague who said one sentence too many at a dinner.
A secret kept inside a family for a generation — and the day someone finally said it out loud.
A spy, a witness or a whistle-blower whose life depended on never being named.
A promise you made to yourself — and the moment you found out whether you could keep it.

final: The snow woman spares him twice — once for his youth, once for his children. Is she more merciful than most humans in stories like this? Than most humans in life?
Would the story be stronger or weaker if she had carried out her threat?
Every marriage has things that are not said. Is that dishonesty, or wisdom?
Before you go — from memory: give me a warning with if you ever…, the same warning with should…, and one mixed conditional about Minokichi.
